Massive 1954 Page 721 Dragline Sitting for Decades Walks Again Ahead of Restoration
16 photos
Photo: Scrappy Industries/YouTube
I don't know about you, but I love revival videos. There's something very cool about seeing a classic car spring back to life after sitting for decades. If you're also a fan of such content, I have something special for you today. This revival video is not about a car but a dragline excavator, a large piece of construction equipment.
Yes, it's perhaps a strange thing to see on these pages, but this thing is spectacularly massive. And even though it doesn't have wheels, it does move under its own power. Moreover, this walking dragline is a rare sight, and, following the revival, it became the only one of its kind that's operational.
If you're unfamiliar with dragline (and it's quite alright if that's the case), these heavy-duty excavators emerged in the early 20th century, replacing the steam and power shovels. Unlike standard excavators that push a bucket away from the machine using a hydraulic arm, draglines rely on gravity and wide ropes suspended from a long boom.
Draglines were primarily used in surface mining but were also utilized in major canal projects, dredging, quarries, and civil engineering. Most draglines are replaced by rotary excavators beginning in the 1970s.
Because large draglines are too heavy for tracks or wheels, they move using massive "shoes" on either side. These lift the machine and slide it forward a few feet at a time. The dragline you see here is one of those rigs.
A Page 721 model from 1954, this dragline is directly linked to the man who invented the concept back in the day. That man is John W. Page, who created the first dragline to use in digging the Chicago Canal. Page built the first walking dragline in 1923 and developed the first diesel engine exclusively for dragline use a year later.
Page also invented the arched dragline bucket, which is still commonly used today, while pioneering an archless bucket design in the 1960s. He started his own dragline-building company in 1912.
A medium-sized walking dragline, the Page 721 is about 22 feet (6.7 meters) high, with the tip of its boom sitting at up to 80 feet (24.4 meters) above the ground . With the 125-foot (38-meter) long boom operating at 30 degrees, the overall machine length reaches a whopping 150 feet. It has an operating weight of 325 to 350 short tons (650,000 to 700,000 pounds).
The Page 721 was originally equipped with an in-house-built horizontal V6 engine running at a constant 450 RPM. This dragline, however, had its original mill replaced with a Cummins unit. The 19-liter inline-six diesel powerplant is part of the iconic KT-series family, which became an industry standard for heavy mining in the 1970s.
This walking dragline has been sitting in a sand and gravel pit for about 20 years. This usually means the end of the line for such equipment, but this Page excavator got lucky. The owner decided to donate it to the Historical Construction Equipment Association in Bowling Green, Ohio.
The donating family and the HCEA have an agreement requiring that the association have it running and operating at their grounds, which is why we're witnessing this historic moment. The HCEA sent a team to have Page 721 operating again in order to move it in a position where it could be disassembled.
The dragline would then be moved to Bowling Green piece by piece, with each to be sandblasted and painted before reassembly. When that happens, it will become the only Page 721 in the world that's fully operational. Until that happens, you can see it coming back to life after 20 years in the video below.
And by the way, if you're a fan of old construction equipment, you can donate to help the HCEA move and restore the walking dragline. You can find more info on their website .
